# Motivation and Problem definition 

## Obs \#1: breast cancer subtypes by hormone receptors

Estrogen receptor (ER) protein expression affects breast cancer prognosis [@Early-Breast-Cancer-Trialists-Collaborative-Group-EBCTCG-2011-nxj;@Cancer_Genome_Atlas_Network2012-lx].

* **ER+** (estrogen receptor positive): ~70% of breast cancers
  - Treatment: hormone therapy (e.g., tamoxifen)
  - Better prognosis

* **ER-** (Estrogen Receptor negative): ~30% of breast cancers
  - Treatment: chemotherapy
  - More aggressive, poor outcomes

## Obs \#2: age and menopause effects on estrogen

Menopause (~50 years) dramatically changes estrogen levels

* Pre-menopausal: high circulating estrogen
* Post-menopausal: low circulating estrogen

\vspace{0.3cm}

* Age-correlated gene expression in breast cancer is largely regulated by **endocrine (estrogen) signaling** [@Osako2020-mq]

## Key question: multiple sources of variation

- Can we identify multiple independent disease mechanisms?

- How do they manifest in observed transcriptional profiles?

\vspace{0.3cm}

1. **ER status**: Tumor-intrinsic differences (ER+ vs ER-)
2. **Age**: age effects in general population
3. **Menopause**: pre- vs. post-menopause

\vspace{0.3cm}

They are all correlated... but not necessarily the same

* Post-menopausal but young (e.g., surgical menopause)
* Pre-menopausal but older (late menopause)

\node[observed] (age) {Age};
\node[observed, right=2.5cm of age] (meno) {Meno};
\node[observed, below=2cm of age] (er) {ER};
\node[observed, below=2cm of meno] (expr) {$Y_{g}$};

\draw[->, thick] (age) -- (meno);
\draw[->, thick] (age) -- (er);
\draw[->, thick] (meno) to[bend right=20] (er);
\draw[->, thick] (meno) -- node[right] {$\beta$} (expr);
\draw[->, thick] (er) -- node[below] {$\mu$} (expr);
\draw[->, thick] (age) to[bend right=20] node[right] {$\alpha$} (expr);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

**Observed** variables:

* Age (continuous), Menopause (categorical), ER status (categorical)

* Gene expression matrix $Y_{gi}$ for a gene $g$ in a sample $i$.

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Parameters** (open):

* $\mu$: ER status effect
* $\alpha$: direct age effect
* $\beta$: menopause effect

:::

```{r include=F}
data.dir <- "../data/recount3"
dir.create(data.dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
.file <- file.path(data.dir, "tcga_brca_rse.rds")
```

```{r tcga_brca_via_recount3, message=F, size="small"}
library(recount3) ## install via Bioconductor

if.needed(.file, {
    ## Take TCGA
    tcga.proj <- subset(available_projects(),
                        file_source == "tcga")
    ## Choose BRCA (breast cancer)
    brca.info <- tcga.proj[tcga.proj$project == "BRCA", ]            
    ## Save the object
    rse.brca <- create_rse(brca.info)                                
    saveRDS(rse.brca, .file)
})
## We can quickly read in `.rds` in the memory
rse <- readRDS(.file)
```


## Side: a trick to avoid overwriting

```{r eval=F}
if.needed <- 
    function(.file, .code) {
        if(!all(file.exists(unlist(.file)))){ .code }
        stopifnot(all(file.exists(unlist(.file))))
    }
```

## Side: What is `RangedSummarizedExperiment` object?

```
                        samples (columns)
                     ┌─────────────────────┐
                     │  S1   S2   S3  ...  │
               ┌─────┼─────────────────────┤
     genes     │ G1  │  10   25   18  ...  │  ← assays (counts, TPM)
     (rows)    │ G2  │   5   12    8  ...  │
               │ ... │ ...  ...  ...  ...  │
               └─────┴─────────────────────┘

  rowRanges: genomic coordinates (chr, start, end, strand)
  colData:   sample metadata (tumor/normal, clinical info)
```

## Column (sample) data

```{r size="small"}
clinical <-
    colData(rse) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    select(
        sample.id = tcga.tcga_barcode,
        sample.type = tcga.cgc_sample_sample_type,
        age = tcga.gdc_cases.diagnoses.age_at_diagnosis,
        menopause = tcga.xml_menopause_status,
        tumor.stage = tcga.gdc_cases.diagnoses.tumor_stage,
        ER.status = tcga.xml_breast_carcinoma_estrogen_receptor_status,
        PR.status = tcga.xml_breast_carcinoma_progesterone_receptor_status,
        HER2.status = tcga.xml_lab_proc_her2_neu_immunohistochemistry_receptor_status
    ) %>%
    as.data.table()
```

## Age distribution by menopause status

```{r age.by.menopause, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
menopause.comparisons <- list(c("Pre", "Peri"), c("Pre", "Post"),
                               c("Pre", "Indeterminate"), c("Peri", "Post"),
                               c("Peri", "Indeterminate"), c("Post", "Indeterminate"))

clinical %>%
    filter(!is.na(menopause)) %>%
    mutate(age = age / 365.25,
           menopause = case_when(
               grepl("^Pre", menopause) ~ "Pre",
               grepl("^Peri", menopause) ~ "Peri",
               grepl("^Post", menopause) ~ "Post",
               TRUE ~ "Indeterminate"
           ),
           menopause = factor(menopause, levels = c("Pre", "Peri", "Indeterminate", "Post"))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = menopause, y = age, fill = menopause)) +
    geom_violin() +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, fill = "white") +
    stat_compare_means(comparisons = menopause.comparisons,
                       method = "t.test", label = "p.format", size = 6/.pt) +
    labs(x = "Menopause Status", y = "Age at Diagnosis (years)") +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Age distribution by ER status

```{r age.by.er, echo=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=3}
clinical %>%
    filter(ER.status %in% c("Positive", "Negative")) %>%
    mutate(age = age / 365.25) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = ER.status, y = age, fill = ER.status)) +
    geom_violin() +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, fill = "white") +
    stat_compare_means(comparisons = list(c("Positive", "Negative")),
                       method = "t.test", label = "p.format", size = 6/.pt) +
    labs(x = "ER Status", y = "Age at Diagnosis (years)") +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```


## Age distribution by subtype


```{r subtype, include=F}
clinical <- clinical %>%
    mutate(subtype = case_when(
               ER.status == "Negative" &
               PR.status == "Negative" &
               HER2.status == "Negative" ~ "Triple-negative",
               HER2.status == "Positive" ~ "HER2+",
               ER.status == "Positive" | PR.status == "Positive" ~ "Luminal",
               TRUE ~ NA_character_
           ))

table(clinical$subtype)
```

```{r age.by.subtype, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
comparisons <- list(c("Triple-negative", "Luminal"),
                    c("Triple-negative", "HER2+"),
                    c("HER2+", "Luminal"))

clinical %>%
    filter(!is.na(subtype)) %>%
    mutate(age = age / 365.25) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = subtype, y = age, fill = subtype)) +
    geom_violin() +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, fill = "white") +
    stat_compare_means(comparisons = comparisons, method = "t.test",
                       label = "p.format", size = 6/.pt) +
    labs(x = "Subtype", y = "Age at Diagnosis (years)") +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```

\vspace{.5cm}

\centerline{"divide and conquer"}

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

\large

\begin{itemize}
\item<1-> Instead of resolving all the parameters all at once, can we estimate each effect one by one?
\item<2-> Are there any genes \textbf{\color{magenta} significantly changed} as a result of the ER status?
\item<3-> How can we \textbf{\color{magenta} test} any significant changes?
\end{itemize}

:::

# Key concepts

## Recap: random variable (`lect02`)

**Random Variable**

* Mathematical representation of all possible values
* Denoted by uppercase letters: $K$, $X$, $T$
* Represents abstract set of possibilities

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Observed Value**

* Actual result from experiment
* Denoted by lowercase letters: $k$, $x$, $t$
* The specific measurement we obtained

## Probability Distribution (`lect02`)

**Definition**: Map: possible value $\to$ probability

\vspace{0.5cm}

* Describes how frequently different values occur
* Discrete (finite) or continuous (infinite)

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Examples**:

* Discrete: Binomial, Poisson

* Continuous: Normal (Gaussian) distribution

## Common Discrete Distributions

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=3, echo=F}
# Set up parameters for different discrete distributions
x_range <- 0:20

                                        # Discrete Uniform (on 1 to 10)
uniform_x <- 1:10
p1 <- data.frame(x = uniform_x, pmf = rep(1/10, 10)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pmf)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
    labs(title = "Discrete Uniform(1,10)",
         x = "x", y = "P(X = x)") +
    ylim(0, 0.4) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size=6))

## Binomial
binom_n <- 20
binom_p <- 0.3
p2 <- data.frame(x = 0:binom_n,
                 pmf = dbinom(0:binom_n, size = binom_n, prob = binom_p)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pmf)) +
    geom_col(fill = "coral", width = 0.7) +
    labs(title = paste0("Binomial(n=", binom_n, ", p=", binom_p, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "P(X = x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size=6))

## Poisson
pois_lambda <- 6
p3 <- data.frame(x = x_range,
                 pmf = dpois(x_range, lambda = pois_lambda)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pmf)) +
    geom_col(fill = "darkgreen", width = 0.7) +
    labs(title = paste0("Poisson(λ=", pois_lambda, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "P(X = x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size=6))

## Geometric
geom_p <- 0.3
p4 <- data.frame(x = x_range,
                 pmf = dgeom(x_range, prob = geom_p)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pmf)) +
    geom_col(fill = "purple", width = 0.7) +
    labs(title = paste0("Geometric(p=", geom_p, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "P(X = x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size=6))

## Negative Binomial
nb_r <- 5
nb_p <- 0.5
p5 <- data.frame(x = x_range,
                 pmf = dnbinom(x_range, size = nb_r, prob = nb_p)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pmf)) +
    geom_col(fill = "orange", width = 0.7) +
    labs(title = paste0("Negative Binomial\n(r=", nb_r, ", p=", nb_p, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "P(X = x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size=6))

                                        # Hypergeometric
hyper_m <- 50  # success states in population
hyper_n <- 50  # failure states in population
hyper_k <- 20  # number of draws
p6 <- data.frame(x = x_range,
                 pmf = dhyper(x_range, m = hyper_m, n = hyper_n, k = hyper_k)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pmf)) +
    geom_col(fill = "darkred", width = 0.7) +
    labs(title = paste0("Hypergeometric\n(m=", hyper_m, ", n=", hyper_n, ", k=", hyper_k, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "P(X = x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size=6))

## Arrange all plots in a 2x3 grid
(p1 | p2 | p3) / (p4 | p5 | p6)
```

## Common Continuous Distributions

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=3, echo=F}
# Set up x range for continuous distributions
x_cont <- seq(-4, 10, length.out = 500)

## Continuous Uniform
unif_a <- 0
unif_b <- 5
c1 <- data.frame(x = x_cont) %>%
    filter(x >= unif_a - 1 & x <= unif_b + 1) %>%
    mutate(pdf = dunif(x, min = unif_a, max = unif_b)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pdf)) +
    geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = paste0("Continuous Uniform\n(a=", unif_a, ", b=", unif_b, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size = 6))

## Normal
norm_mu <- 0
norm_sd <- 1
c2 <- data.frame(x = x_cont) %>%
    mutate(pdf = dnorm(x, mean = norm_mu, sd = norm_sd)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pdf)) +
    geom_line(color = "coral", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = paste0("Normal(μ=", norm_mu, ", σ=", norm_sd, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size = 6))

## Exponential
exp_rate <- 0.5
c3 <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 500)) %>%
    mutate(pdf = dexp(x, rate = exp_rate)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pdf)) +
    geom_line(color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = paste0("Exponential(λ=", exp_rate, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size = 6))

## Gamma
gamma_shape <- 2
gamma_rate <- 1
c4 <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 500)) %>%
    mutate(pdf = dgamma(x, shape = gamma_shape, rate = gamma_rate)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pdf)) +
    geom_line(color = "purple", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = paste0("Gamma(α=", gamma_shape, ", β=", gamma_rate, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size = 6))

## Beta
beta_a <- 2
beta_b <- 5
c5 <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 500)) %>%
    mutate(pdf = dbeta(x, shape1 = beta_a, shape2 = beta_b)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pdf)) +
    geom_line(color = "orange", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = paste0("Beta(α=", beta_a, ", β=", beta_b, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size = 6))

## Chi-squared
chisq_df <- 4
c6 <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 15, length.out = 500)) %>%
    mutate(pdf = dchisq(x, df = chisq_df)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pdf)) +
    geom_line(color = "darkred", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = paste0("Chi-squared(df=", chisq_df, ")"),
         x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8), axis.text = element_text(size = 6))

## Arrange all plots in a 2x3 grid
(c1 | c2 | c3) / (c4 | c5 | c6)
```

## What is Hypothesis Testing?

A formal procedure for making decisions based on finite data samples

**Key question**: Is the observed effect real, or could it have occurred by chance?

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Applications in genomics**:

* Is a gene differentially expressed between conditions?
* Are two genetic variants associated with a trait?
* Does a drug treatment have an effect on gene expression?

## First hypothesis test: The Lady Tasting Tea

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.6}

* Dr. Muriel Bristol claimed she could tell whether milk or tea was poured first into a cup

* RA Fisher designed a randomized control experiment:
  - 8 cups of tea (4 milk-first, 4 tea-first)
  - Dr. Bristol tasted all 8 cups
  - She had to identify which 4 were milk-first

:::
::: {.column width=.3}

![](img/Nice_Cup_of_Tea.jpg)

:::
::::::

\vspace{0.3cm}

**The question**: Could she really tell the difference, or was she just guessing?

* $H_0$: She's guessing (no ability)
* If guessing, probability of getting all 4 correct by chance = $1/\binom{8}{4} \approx 0.014$
<!-- \vspace{0.3cm} -->
<!-- **Result**: She correctly identified all 8 cups! -->
<!-- \vspace{0.3cm} -->
<!-- **This experiment** laid the foundation for modern hypothesis testing -->

\vfill

\small

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_tasting_tea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_tasting_tea)

## Let's focus on how $X$ affects $Y$ in the full PGM

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    node distance=.2cm,
    observed/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!30, minimum size=0cm},
    latent/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!0, minimum size=0cm}
]
\node[observed] (er) {$X_{i}$};
\node[latent, right=1cm of er] (mu) {$\mu_{g}$};
\node[observed, below=1cm of er] (expr) {$Y_{ig}$};
\draw[->, thick] (er) -- (expr);
\draw[->, thick] (mu) -- (expr);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

:::
::: {.column width=.55}

\large

* $X_{i}$ for each $i \in [n]$:

$$X_{i} = 
\left\{\begin{array}{ll} 
	0 & \text{if ER+} \\
	1 & \text{if ER-}
\end{array}
\right.$$

* We can say gene expression $Y_{ig}$ changes as a function of $X$ by a gene $g$'s $\mu_{g}$

* What would be the probability distribution of $Y$?

:::
::::::

## How **significantly** $X$ affects $Y$?

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    node distance=.2cm,
    observed/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!30, minimum size=0cm},
    latent/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!0, minimum size=0cm}
]
\node[observed] (er0) {$X_{i} = 0$};
\node[latent, right=.5cm of er0] (mu0) {$\mu_{g0}$};
\node[observed, below=1cm of er0] (expr0) {$Y_{ig}$};
\node[observed, right=4cm of er0] (er1) {$X_{i} = 1$};
\node[latent, right=.5cm of er1] (mu1) {$\mu_{g1}$};
\node[observed, below=1cm of er1] (expr1) {$Y_{ig}$};
\draw[->, thick] (er0) -- (expr0);
\draw[->, thick] (mu0) -- (expr0);
\draw[->, thick] (er1) -- (expr1);
\draw[->, thick] (mu1) -- (expr1);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\vfill

\large

\only<1>{

Here, we show the "data-generating" scheme more explicitly.

}

\only<2>{
\begin{enumerate}
\item Has this gene $g$ been affected by ER? 
\item $Y_{g}$ changes depending on $X=0$ or $X=1$? 
\item Is $\mu_{g0} = \mu_{g1}$?
\end{enumerate}
}

\only<3>{
Formal writing of hypothesis testing:
$$H_{0}: \mu_{g0} = \mu_{g1} \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_{1}: \mu_{g0} \neq \mu_{g1}$$
}

\normalsize

# An example of hypothesis testing

## Five Steps of Hypothesis Testing

\Large

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

\begin{enumerate}
\item<1-> \textbf{\color{teal} Choose Test statistic}
\item<2-> Establish Null Hypothesis ($H_0$)
\item<3-> Define "rejection" region
\end{enumerate}

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

\onslide<4>{

4. Compute Test Statistic

5. Make a decision

\vspace{1cm}

\centerline{straightforward}

}

:::
::::::

\vfill

\onslide<3->{
For Step 1-3: What would happen **under the null**?
}

## How to come up with test statistic?

\Large

* Decide on the effect of interest

* Design experiment or study

* \textbf{\color{teal} Modelling can guide us}

* Choose a data summary function and test statistic

## Choose test statistic: How **significantly** $X$ affects $Y$?

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    node distance=.2cm,
    observed/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!30, minimum size=0cm},
    latent/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!0, minimum size=0cm}
]
\node[observed] (er0) {$X_{i} = 0$};
\node[latent, right=.5cm of er0] (mu0) {$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g0}$};
\node[observed, below=1cm of er0] (expr0) {$Y_{ig}$};
\node[observed, right=2cm of er0] (er1) {$X_{i} = 1$};
\node[latent, right=.5cm of er1] (mu1) {$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g1}$};
\node[observed, below=1cm of er1] (expr1) {$Y_{ig}$};
\draw[->, thick] (er0) -- (expr0);
\draw[->, thick] (mu0) -- (expr0);
\draw[->, thick] (er1) -- (expr1);
\draw[->, thick] (mu1) -- (expr1);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\large

$$H_{0}: \mu_{g1} = \mu_{g0} \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_{1}: \mu_{g1} \neq \mu_{g0} $$

\normalsize

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

\large

\begin{enumerate}
\item<1-> What's our interest?
\item<2-> The difference of the "average" parameters
\item<3> How can we estimate the mean (1st moment) from data?
\end{enumerate}
\onslide<3>{
$$\{Y_{1g},\ldots,Y_{ng}\}$$
}

\normalsize
:::
::::::

## Step 1. Choose Test Statistics

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    node distance=.2cm,
    observed/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!30, minimum size=0cm},
    latent/.style={circle, draw, fill=gray!0, minimum size=0cm}
]
\node[observed] (er0) {$X_{i} = 0$};
\node[latent, right=.5cm of er0] (mu0) {$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g0}$};
\node[observed, below=1cm of er0] (expr0) {$Y_{ig}$};
\node[observed, right=2cm of er0] (er1) {$X_{i} = 1$};
\node[latent, right=.5cm of er1] (mu1) {$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g1}$};
\node[observed, below=1cm of er1] (expr1) {$Y_{ig}$};
\draw[->, thick] (er0) -- (expr0);
\draw[->, thick] (mu0) -- (expr0);
\draw[->, thick] (er1) -- (expr1);
\draw[->, thick] (mu1) -- (expr1);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\large

$$H_{0}: \mu_{g1} = \mu_{g0} \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_{1}: \mu_{g1} \neq \mu_{g0} $$

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

\large

* Sample mean for $X_{i}=0$

$$\bar{Y}_{g0} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1- X_{i}) Y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - X_{i})}$$

* Sample mean for $X_{i}=1$

$$\bar{Y}_{g1} =\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i} Y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}}$$

:::
::::::

```{r plot.functions, include=FALSE}
# Modular function to create gene expression data frame
get.expr.data <- function(gene_name, rse, clinical) {
    # Find gene
    gene_idx <- which(rowData(rse)$gene_name == gene_name)

    if (length(gene_idx) == 0) {
        stop(sprintf("Gene %s not found", gene_name))
    }

    # Extract expression (log2 transformed)
    gene_expr <- log2(assay(rse)[gene_idx, ] + 1)

    # Create data frame with X and Y
    .df <- clinical %>%
        filter(ER.status %in% c("Positive", "Negative")) %>%
        mutate(
            X = ifelse(ER.status == "Negative", 1, 0),
            Y = gene_expr[match(sample.id, colData(rse)$tcga.tcga_barcode)]
        ) %>%
        filter(!is.na(Y))

    return(.df)
}

# Modular function to plot gene expression density by ER status
plot.gene.density <- function(gene_name, gene_data) {
    # Calculate sample means
    .means <- gene_data %>%
        group_by(X) %>%
        summarise(mean_Y = mean(Y)) %>%
        mutate(X_label = ifelse(X == 0, "X = 0\n(ER Negative)", "X = 1\n(ER Positive)"))

    # Create density plots
    gene_data %>%
        mutate(X_label = ifelse(X == 0, "X = 0\n(ER Negative)", "X = 1\n(ER Positive)")) %>%
        ggplot(aes(x = Y, fill = factor(X))) +
        geom_density(alpha = 0.7) +
        geom_vline(data = .means, aes(xintercept = mean_Y),
                   linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1, color = "black") +
        facet_grid(X_label ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
        labs(x = sprintf("%s Expression: Y = log2(count + 1)", gene_name),
             y = "Density",
             title = sprintf("Distribution of %s Expression by ER Status", gene_name)) +
        scale_fill_manual(values = c("0" = "#E69F00", "1" = "#56B4E9"),
                         labels = c("ER Negative", "ER Positive")) +
        theme_classic() +
        theme(legend.position = "right",
              legend.title = element_blank(),
              strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"),
              strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0))
}

# Modular function to plot t-distribution with test results
plot.gene.tdist <- function(gene_name, gene_data, color = "#E41A1C", show.label = F) {
    # Perform t-test
    gene_test <- t.test(Y ~ X, data = gene_data, var.equal = TRUE)
    t_stat <- gene_test$statistic
    df <- gene_test$parameter
    p_value <- gene_test$p.value

    # Generate t-distribution
    t_range <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 500)
    t_density <- dt(t_range, df = df)
    t_df <- data.frame(t = t_range, density = t_density)

    # Create label data frames for ggrepel
    label_obs <- data.frame(
        x = t_stat,
        y = max(t_density) * 0.8,
        label = sprintf("Observed\nt = %.2f\np = %.3f", t_stat, p_value)
    )

    label_crit <- data.frame(
        x = qt(0.975, df),
        y = max(t_density) * 0.3,
        label = sprintf("α/2 = 0.025\nt = %.2f", qt(0.975, df))
    )

    ret <- ggplot(t_df, aes(x = t, y = density)) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "black") +
        ## Shade rejection regions (two-tailed, alpha = 0.05)
        geom_area(data = subset(t_df, t < qt(0.025, df)),
                  aes(x = t, y = density), fill = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
        geom_area(data = subset(t_df, t > qt(0.975, df)),
                  aes(x = t, y = density), fill = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
        ## Mark critical values
        geom_vline(xintercept = qt(c(0.025, 0.975), df),
                   linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +

        ## Mark observed t-statistic
        geom_vline(xintercept = t_stat,
                   linetype = "solid", color = color, linewidth = 1.5) +
        labs(x = "t-statistic", y = "Density",
             title = sprintf("%s: t-distribution (df = %d) under H₀: μ₁ = μ₀", gene_name, df)) +
        theme_classic() +
        theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
              plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "darkgray"))

    if(show.label){
        ## Add labels with ggrepel
        ret <-
            ret +
            geom_label_repel(data = label_obs, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
                             color = color, fontface = "bold", size = 3,
                             box.padding = 0.5, point.padding = 0.5,
                             segment.color = color, segment.size = 0.5,
                             min.segment.length = 0) +
            geom_label_repel(data = label_crit, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
                             color = "red", size = 2.5,
                             box.padding = 0.5, point.padding = 0.5,
                             segment.color = "red", segment.size = 0.5,
                             min.segment.length = 0)
    }

    ret
}
```

## Compare variance: _ESR1_ vs. _BEST1_

```{r variance.comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3}
# Combine ESR1 and BEST1 data
.df_combined <- bind_rows(
    .df_esr1 %>% mutate(gene = "ESR1"),
    .df_best1 %>% mutate(gene = "BEST1")
)

# Calculate means and SDs for each gene
.stats <- .df_combined %>%
    group_by(gene) %>%
    summarise(
        mean_Y = mean(Y),
        sd_Y = sd(Y),
        var_Y = var(Y)
    )

# Create marginal density plots with mean and ±1 SD marked
.df_combined %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = Y, fill = gene)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
    # Add mean lines
    geom_vline(data = .stats, aes(xintercept = mean_Y, color = gene),
               linetype = "solid", linewidth = 1) +
    # Add ±1 SD regions
    geom_rect(data = .stats,
              aes(xmin = mean_Y - sd_Y, xmax = mean_Y + sd_Y,
                  ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = gene),
              alpha = 0.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    # Add labels
    geom_text(data = .stats,
              aes(x = mean_Y, y = 0.2,
                  label = sprintf("μ = %.2f\nσ = %.2f",
                                mean_Y, sd_Y),
                  color = gene),
              vjust = 0, hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
    facet_grid(gene~.) +
    labs(x = "Expression: Y = log2(count + 1)",
         y = "Density",
         title = "Variance Comparison: ESR1 vs BEST1 (Marginal Distributions)") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("ESR1" = "#E41A1C", "BEST1" = "#377EB8")) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("ESR1" = "#E41A1C", "BEST1" = "#377EB8")) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"))
```

## Revised Test Statistic - should adjust T by variance

\huge

$$T = \frac{ \bar{Y}_{g1} - \bar{Y}_{g0} } { \sqrt{ \mathbb{V}\!\left[\bar{Y}_{g1} - \bar{Y}_{g0}\right] } }$$

\normalsize

## Side note: Test statistic is a random variable

In this example,

$$T = \frac{ \bar{Y}_{g1} - \bar{Y}_{g0} } { \sqrt{ \mathbb{V}\!\left[\bar{Y}_{g1} - \bar{Y}_{g0}\right] } }$$


- $Y$ is a random variable

- And the sample mean is a function of $Y$ (also, random variable)

- In general, if $X$ is a random variable, a function take on $X$, i.e., $g(X)$, is also a random variable. 

## Five Steps of Hypothesis Testing

\Large

\begin{enumerate}
\item Choose Test statistic
\item \textbf{\color{teal} Establish Null Hypothesis ($H_0$)}
\item Define "rejection" region
\item Compute Test Statistic
\item Make a decision
\end{enumerate}

\normalsize

## Step 2. Estimate/simulate null Distribution

**Definition**: The probability distribution of a test statistic when $H_0$ is true

\vspace{0.5cm}

* Represents expected outcomes if there were **no real effect**
* Used as baseline for comparison
* Allows us to assess how "extreme" our observed data is

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Idea**: 

* If observed statistic is unlikely under null distribution, we have evidence against $H_0$

* Under the null hypothesis $H_{0}$, what would be the distribution of test statistic $T$?

## How do we estimate the distribution of $T$?

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

**Option 1: Theoretical**

\small

* Make distributional assumptions
* Derive the null distribution mathematically
* Use known probability distributions

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Example**: t-distribution

* Assume normality
* Use Central Limit Theorem
* Analytical formula available

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Pros**: Fast, well-studied

**Cons**: Requires assumptions

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

**Option 2: Empirical**

\small

* Simulate/resample data
* Generate null distribution empirically
* No distributional assumptions needed

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Example**: Permutation test

* Randomly shuffle group labels
* Recalculate test statistic
* Repeat many times

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Pros**: Assumption-free

**Cons**: Computationally intensive

:::
::::::

## Option 1: Theoretical approach (t-distribution)

**For ESR1 gene**:

```{r theoretical.esr1, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
# Perform t-test using theoretical t-distribution
t.test(Y ~ X, data = .df_esr1, var.equal = TRUE)
```

\vspace{0.3cm}

**How it works**:

1. Assume $Y_{ig} \sim N(\mu_g, \sigma^2)$
2. Under $H_0$: $T = \frac{\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0}{s_{\text{pooled}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_0} + \frac{1}{n_1}}} \sim t_{n_0+n_1-2}$
3. Look up p-value from $t$-distribution tables/functions

## Option 2: Empirical approach (Permutation test)

**For ESR1 gene**:

```{r permutation.setup, include=FALSE}
# Function to perform permutation test
perm.test <- function(gene_data, n_perm = 10000) {
    # Observed test statistic
    obs_diff <- mean(gene_data$Y[gene_data$X == 1]) - mean(gene_data$Y[gene_data$X == 0])

    # Permutation distribution
    perm_diffs <- replicate(n_perm, {
        # Shuffle group labels
        shuffled_X <- sample(gene_data$X)
        # Recalculate difference
        mean(gene_data$Y[shuffled_X == 1]) - mean(gene_data$Y[shuffled_X == 0])
    })

    # Calculate p-value (two-tailed)
    p_value <- mean(abs(perm_diffs) >= abs(obs_diff))

    return(list(
        obs_diff = obs_diff,
        perm_diffs = perm_diffs,
        p_value = p_value
    ))
}
```

```{r permutation.esr1, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
# Permutation test for ESR1
set.seed(123)
perm_result <- perm.test(.df_esr1, n_perm = 10000)
```

\vspace{0.3cm}

**How it works**:

1. Calculate observed difference: $T_{\text{obs}} = \bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0$
2. Shuffle group labels (X) many times
3. Recalculate $T$ for each shuffle
4. P-value = proportion of shuffles with $|T| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|$

## Comparing approaches: ESR1 (significant gene)

```{r compare.esr1, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=2.5}
# Run permutation test for ESR1
set.seed(123)
perm_esr1 <- perm.test(.df_esr1, n_perm = 10000)

# Get theoretical t-test results
t_esr1 <- t.test(Y ~ X, data = .df_esr1, var.equal = TRUE)

# Create comparison plot
p1 <- data.frame(t = perm_esr1$perm_diffs) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = t)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50, fill = "gray70", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = perm_esr1$obs_diff, color = "#E41A1C", linewidth = 1.5) +
    labs(title = "Empirical: Permutation distribution",
         x = "Mean difference (ER+ - ER-)",
         y = "Density") +
    theme_classic()

p2 <- plot.gene.tdist("ESR1", .df_esr1, color = "#E41A1C") +
    labs(title = "Theoretical: t-distribution")

p1 | p2
```

**ESR1**: Both approaches agree - highly significant (p < 0.001)

## Comparing approaches: BEST1 (non-significant gene)

```{r compare.best1, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=2.5}
# Run permutation test for BEST1
set.seed(456)
perm_best1 <- perm.test(.df_best1, n_perm = 10000)

# Get theoretical t-test results
t_best1 <- t.test(Y ~ X, data = .df_best1, var.equal = TRUE)

# Create comparison plot
p1 <- data.frame(t = perm_best1$perm_diffs) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = t)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50, fill = "gray70", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = perm_best1$obs_diff, color = "#377EB8", linewidth = 1.5) +
    labs(title = "Empirical: Permutation distribution",
         x = "Mean difference (ER+ - ER-)",
         y = "Density") +
    theme_classic()

p2 <- plot.gene.tdist("BEST1", .df_best1, color = "#377EB8") +
    labs(title = "Theoretical: t-distribution")

p1 | p2
```

**BEST1**: Both approaches agree - not significant (p > 0.05)

## When to use which approach?

:::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=.45}

**Theoretical (t-distribution)**

\small

**Use when**:

* Sample size is moderate to large
* Data is approximately normal
* Speed is important
* Need confidence intervals

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Advantages**:

* Fast computation
* Well-established theory
* Standard in literature

:::
::: {.column width=.45}

**Empirical (Permutation)**

\small

**Use when**:

* Sample size is small
* Data is non-normal
* Variance assumptions violated
* Custom test statistics

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Advantages**:

* No distribution assumptions
* Exact p-values (for small samples)
* Flexible

:::
::::::


## Five Steps of Hypothesis Testing

\Large

\begin{enumerate}
\item Choose Test statistic
\item Establish Null Hypothesis ($H_0$)
\item \textbf{\color{teal} Define "rejection" region}
\item \textbf{\color{teal} Compute Test Statistic}
\item Make a decision
\end{enumerate}

\normalsize

## Step 3. Define the rejection region

**Definition**: Set of test statistic values where we reject $H_0$

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Determined by**:

* **Significance level ($\alpha$)**: Acceptable false positive rate (typically 0.05)
* **Power considerations**: Maximize probability of detecting true effects
* **Alternative hypothesis type**:
  * Two-sided tests: Split rejection region between both tails
  * One-sided tests: Concentrate region on one tail

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Choice reflects**: What values provide "sufficient evidence" against $H_0$

## Step 4. Two-sample t-statistic by sample mean \& var.

1. **Calculate sample means** for each group:

$$\bar{Y}_0 = \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i: X_i=0} Y_i \quad \text{and} \quad \bar{Y}_1 = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i: X_i=1} Y_i$$

\vspace{0.3cm}

2. **Calculate sample variances** for each group:

$$s_0^2 = \frac{1}{n_0-1}\sum_{i: X_i=0} (Y_i - \bar{Y}_0)^2 \quad \text{and} \quad s_1^2 = \frac{1}{n_1-1}\sum_{i: X_i=1} (Y_i - \bar{Y}_1)^2$$

\vspace{0.3cm}

## Step 4. Two-sample t-statistic - continued

3. **Calculate pooled variance** (assuming equal variance):

$$s_{\text{pooled}}^2 = \frac{(n_0-1)s_0^2 + (n_1-1)s_1^2}{n_0 + n_1 - 2}$$

\vspace{0.3cm}

4. **Compute the t-statistic**:

$$T = \frac{\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0}{s_{\text{pooled}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_0} + \frac{1}{n_1}}}$$

## In practice, use a built-in `t.test` function

\small

```
t.test                  package:stats                  R Documentation

Student's t-Test

Description:

     Performs one and two sample t-tests on vectors of data.

Usage:

     t.test(x, ...)
```

## In practice, for many hypotheses, `matrixTests`

\small

```
ttest               package:matrixTests                R Documentation

t-test

Description:

     Performs a t-test on each row/column of the input matrix.

Usage:

     row_t_equalvar(x, y, null = 0, alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
```

## P-value

**Definition**: Probability of observing a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than observed, assuming $H_0$ is true

\vspace{0.5cm}

* Scaled to range $[0, 1]$
* Smaller p-values = stronger evidence against $H_0$
* Common threshold: $p < 0.05$ for "statistical significance"

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Important**:

* p-value is NOT the probability that $H_0$ is true
* It's the probability of the data (or more extreme), given $H_0$


## Five Steps of Hypothesis Testing

\Large

\begin{enumerate}
\item Choose Test statistic
\item Establish Null Hypothesis ($H_0$)
\item Define "rejection" region
\item Compute Test Statistic
\item \textbf{\color{teal} Make a decision }
\end{enumerate}

\normalsize

## Interpreting p-values

Which of the following are true? (select all that apply)

 a. If the effect size is very small, but the sample size is large enough, it is possible to have a statistically significant p-value
 b. A study may show a relatively large magnitude of association (effect size), but a statistically insignificant p-value if the sample size is small
 c. A very small p-value indicates there is a very small chance the finding is a false positive

# Discussion


## Types of Errors

|                    | $H_0$ True         | $H_0$ False          |
|--------------------|--------------------|----------------------|
| **Reject $H_0$**   | Type I Error ($\alpha$) | Correct (Power)      |
| **Fail to reject** | Correct            | Type II Error ($\beta$) |

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Type I Error (False Positive)**

* Reject $H_0$ when it's actually true
* Controlled by significance level $\alpha$

**Type II Error (False Negative)**

* Fail to reject $H_0$ when it's actually false
* Related to power: Power = $1 - \beta$

## Visualizing Type I and Type II Errors

```{r type.errors.viz, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3}
# Parameters for null and alternative distributions
mu_0 <- 0          # Mean under H0
mu_1 <- 2          # Mean under H1 (effect size)
sigma <- 1         # Standard deviation
alpha <- 0.05      # Significance level

# Critical value for two-tailed test
critical_value <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2, mean = mu_0, sd = sigma)

# Generate data for plotting
x <- seq(-4, 6, length.out = 500)
y_null <- dnorm(x, mean = mu_0, sd = sigma)
y_alt <- dnorm(x, mean = mu_1, sd = sigma)

# Create data frame
df_plot <- data.frame(
    x = rep(x, 2),
    density = c(y_null, y_alt),
    distribution = rep(c("H₀: μ = 0 (Null)", "H₁: μ = 2 (Alternative)"), each = length(x))
)

# Calculate beta (Type II error)
beta <- pnorm(critical_value, mean = mu_1, sd = sigma)
power <- 1 - beta

# Create the plot
ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = x, y = density, color = distribution, linetype = distribution)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +

    # Type I error (alpha) - right tail of null
    geom_area(data = subset(df_plot, distribution == "H₀: μ = 0 (Null)" & x > critical_value),
              aes(x = x, y = density), fill = "red", alpha = 0.3, inherit.aes = FALSE) +

    # Type II error (beta) - left tail of alternative
    geom_area(data = subset(df_plot, distribution == "H₁: μ = 2 (Alternative)" & x < critical_value),
              aes(x = x, y = density), fill = "orange", alpha = 0.3, inherit.aes = FALSE) +

    # Power - right tail of alternative
    geom_area(data = subset(df_plot, distribution == "H₁: μ = 2 (Alternative)" & x > critical_value),
              aes(x = x, y = density), fill = "green", alpha = 0.3, inherit.aes = FALSE) +

    # Critical value line
    geom_vline(xintercept = critical_value, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +

    # Add labels
    annotate("text", x = critical_value + 0.3, y = max(y_null) * 0.95,
             label = sprintf("Critical value\n(α = %.2f)", alpha),
             hjust = 0, size = 3) +

    annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 0.15,
             label = sprintf("Type I Error\nα = %.2f", alpha),
             color = "red", fontface = "bold", size = 3) +

    annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.08,
             label = sprintf("Type II Error\nβ = %.2f", beta),
             color = "orange", fontface = "bold", size = 3) +

    annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 0.05,
             label = sprintf("Power\n1-β = %.2f", power),
             color = "darkgreen", fontface = "bold", size = 3) +

    scale_color_manual(values = c("H₀: μ = 0 (Null)" = "blue",
                                   "H₁: μ = 2 (Alternative)" = "darkgreen")) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("H₀: μ = 0 (Null)" = "solid",
                                      "H₁: μ = 2 (Alternative)" = "dashed")) +

    labs(x = "Test Statistic", y = "Density",
         title = "Type I Error, Type II Error, and Statistical Power",
         color = "Distribution", linetype = "Distribution") +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(legend.position = "top",
          legend.text = element_text(size = 9))
```

**Key**: Red = Type I error (α), Orange = Type II error (β), Green = Power (1-β)

## Statistical Power

**Definition**: Probability of correctly rejecting a false $H_0$

\vspace{0.5cm}

* Measures ability to detect real effects when they exist
* Power = $1 - \beta$, where $\beta$ is Type II error rate

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Factors affecting power**:

* Sample size (larger $\rightarrow$ higher power)
* Effect size (larger $\rightarrow$ higher power)
* Significance level $\alpha$ (larger $\rightarrow$ higher power)
* Variability in data (lower $\rightarrow$ higher power)


## Common p-value pitfalls

A p-value is **NOT**:

- The probability that the null hypothesis is true

- The probability that the finding is a "fluke"

- A measure of the size or importance of observed effects


## Different kinds of *t*-tests:

- One sample *or* **two samples**

- One-sided *or* **two sided**

- Paired *or* **unpaired**

- Equal variance *or* unequal variance

## Common Non-parametric Tests

**Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Mann-Whitney U)**

* Non-parametric alternative to two-sample t-test
* Tests if two distributions differ
\vspace{0.5cm}

**Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test**

* Non-parametric alternative to paired t-test
\vspace{0.5cm}

**Permutation Tests**

* Simulate null distribution

## Final quiz: True or False

\large

* Modelling doesn't help us design hypothesis testing

* We need complete knowledge to come up with a working hypothesis

* p-value is the evidence for the null hypothesis

* A small p-value suggests our alternative hypothesis $H_1$ is true

* It is highly recommended to implement my own hypothesis tests

* Hypothesis testing is an ultimate scientific proof

## Some aspect of scientific explanation

\large

> "Explaining a contrast is sometimes easier than explaining the fact"

\vfill

\centerline{"P rather than Q" vs. "P" or "Q" alone}

## Summary

\large

* Modelling $\implies$ expose a specific hypothesis

* We may **NOT** have complete knowledge before hypothesis

* Testing **ONLY** reject the null hypothesis

* Use existing (`R`) hypothesis test functions whenever possible
